title: Large language models that replace human participants can harmfully misportray and flatten identity groups

bias_targets.methodology: Prompting LLMs with specific racial identities (Black, White, Asian) and comparing their open-ended and discretized responses to human in-group and out-group participants using n-gram Jaccard distance, SBERT embeddings, and multiple-choice distributions to assess misportrayal and group flattening.

Prompting LLMs with explicit gender identities (women, men, non-binary people) and comparing their text responses against human baselines using similarity and diversity metrics to measure how models misportray and homogeneously flatten these groups.

Prompting LLMs with generational personas (Baby Boomer, Millennial, Generation Z) and comparing their free-text outputs to human survey responses to evaluate out-group stereotyping (misportrayal) and lack of response variance (flattening).

Prompting LLMs with disability identities (ADD/ADHD, impaired vision, no disability) and comparing generated text to human participant data to measure whether models generate out-group imitations rather than authentic in-group perspectives.

Using explicit demographic labels and identity-coded names representing intersectional identities (e.g., Black women, White men) to prompt LLMs, then comparing the semantic distance and diversity of their responses to actual intersectional human demographics.
